paragraphs: I studied abroad for two months at the University of North Carolina, a state university in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on the East Coast of the United States. The University of North Carolina Hospitals are widely known as a hospital whose primary care is among the best in the US. Because of limits on course capacity, I could not take family medicine or emergency medicine, which focus on primary care, so I decided to take departments that I would have little chance to see in Japan, and I did my clerkships in infectious diseases and pediatric neurology instead. Below I write my report on the clerkships I experienced there, in chronological order. First, the first month was my clerkship in infectious diseases. There were also a ward team and outpatient clinics, but I basically belonged to the consult team for most of the time. The clerkship in infectious diseases went as follows. At 9 a.m. everyone gathered in the infectious diseases office to check whether there were any new patient consults. If there was a new patient, the resident, the intern and the students each contacted the fellow and took charge of the patient. For the first two weeks or so, I chose patients myself from the electronic medical record, went to take their histories, was allowed to do the physical examination, and summarised it in a report that I submitted to the fellow. Since my first goal was to get used to the work, I spent about an hour and a half, and up to two hours at the longest, on each patient, concentrating on obtaining all the necessary and sufficient information. In the afternoon, from 1:30 every day, each person gave a case presentation to the attending in the conference room, and after sharing patient information we did rounds. The infectious diseases team was large: one attending, two fellows, one resident or intern, three medical students, one pharmacist, one pharmacy resident and two pharmacy students. The pharmacists were especially enthusiastic about teaching students, gave me lectures and even gave me an electronic textbook. Also, a fourth-year student was doing the clerkship with me, so I often asked him about things I did not know or did not understand, and then studied by looking them up on UpToDate. Of course, for advanced matters, I tried to understand by asking the other senior doctors. At first, many of the infectious diseases and antibiotics were unfamiliar, so listening to the conferences took a lot of effort, but after the first two weeks I could understand most of the content. For the following two weeks, I asked them to pass any newly consulted patients to me, but the number of consults was very small and I could hardly see any patients directly. Instead, I think I often attended the case conference held every day from 10 a.m. and the M&M conference. Since I had no chance to give a case presentation, I asked on the last day if I could give a presentation, and they readily agreed. The theme was HTLV-1, an infectious disease of Japan, and both the attending and the fellows listened with enthusiasm, and we had a lively discussion, which was a valuable experience. What I gained through the month in infectious diseases was the realisation that if I try desperately to convey something, the other person will always understand. At first I was worried about whether my English would be understood, but I found that if I conveyed what I wanted to say clearly with gestures, I could get through, and this gave me great confidence. And by exchanging casual conversation with people regardless of their occupation, I was able to build good relationships with paramedical staff and patients. Through communicating with people, I could understand what an American hospital is like and what the character of North Carolina and its people is like, and I was able to blend in naturally, so as a start the first month was very satisfying. In the second month I did my clerkship in pediatric neurology. The timing of my enrolment was good, and I had the great chance to do the clerkship together with local third-year students. Having just changed departments and not knowing a great deal, I again asked the students I was working with and filled in what I did not understand as I went. I could ask them more easily than the senior doctors, and since they answered from a student's point of view, it was a great help to my understanding. The clerkship in pediatric neurology went as follows. First, I went to the lecture room at 7:30 a.m. and attended the first lecture of the morning for an hour. Despite the early hour, there was not a single student rubbing sleepy eyes, and everyone listened eagerly to understand the content fully. In the lecture style, the teacher explained the basics from a clinical perspective and then the students practised them with each other, or the teacher asked the students questions and had them answer, so it was student-centred. After that I went to the ward, met my own patients and talked with them, and prepared my presentation in under 30 minutes, also using the chart. I tend to go at my own pace, but I think that the time constraint here helped me develop concentration and learn to overcome pressure. I gave my presentation at 9, and after that we did ward rounds. When that ended, there was another one-hour lecture from 12 with lunch. After that, if there was a newly admitted patient, I repeated the training of taking the history and physical examination from scratch and writing it in the chart. I was asked to do far more difficult things than in the first month, and the schedule was dense, so at first I was often confused, but with the help of the students around me and the kind senior doctors I gradually adapted. Above all, what made me glad to have done my clerkship in pediatric neurology was that everyone called me by the nickname Kaz and was friendly with me. Everyone was so friendly that I wondered whether they would be this kind to an international student, and the busy clerkship came to seem easy. On the last day of the pediatric neurology clerkship, the neurology attending held a pizza party, and I enjoyed a meal with the students and senior doctors I had worked with. I tried in my own way to engage in cultural exchange, including as a way of expressing gratitude, by making Japanese food to bring and playing the cello. The third-year student and the fellow who were the closest to me said, "Having Kaz here made it a special month for us," and at that moment, together with a sense of accomplishment in the clerkship, I was overcome by the feeling that I was truly glad to have studied in America. Although it was a short period of two months, every day was a series of discoveries and a challenge to myself, and I think I grew a little by overcoming them. I would like to express my deep gratitude to Dr. 坂本 and Dr. 粕谷, who gave me this opportunity, to everyone in the International Exchange Office and the Student Affairs Office, and to all the others involved in the study abroad program. Thank you very much.
